newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arab foreign ministers gather in Cairo.
newsitem.headline: Arab foreign ministers gather in Cairo.

text.p: Ministers from Egypt, Syria and the six Gulf Arab states started two days of talks in Cairo on Saturday on the Middle East peace process and Gulf security.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa opened the meeting at his ministry with a call for joint Arab action "especially in light of the circumstances the Middle East is going through".

Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara of Syria, the toughest of the eight states towards Israel, told reporters on arrival that the Middle East peace process no longer existed, ignoring reports of a breakthrough on the Israeli-Palestinian track.
"There is no peace process now," the Syrian foreign minister said at Cairo airport.

Syria is expected to argue that the Arab states should respond to the challenge of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government by ending all steps towards normalisation with the Jewish state.

Syria and Israel have not held face-to-face talks for most of this year. Progess on the Syrian track is impossible as long as the Netanyahu government -- which opposes trading occupied Arab land for peace -- refuses to discuss withdrawal from the Golan Heights, captured from Syria in 1967, Syria says.
Moussa, who spent the late morning at the airport receiving the visiting ministers, said the meeting would also discuss cooperation within the eight-state alliance and reactivating the Arab League.
The eight countries, known as the Damascus Declaration states after the agreement they signed after the Gulf War in 1991, meet every six months to keep the alliance alive.
The Gulf states are the members of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) -- Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
Despite Shara's gloomy reply, Moussa referred to a breakthrough in the peace process, saying great progress had been achieved towards signing the long-delayed Hebron agreement.
Hebron is the last of seven major West Bank towns occupied in the 1967 Middle East war that Israel agreed to turn over to the Palestinian Authority under the 1995 self-rule deal.
"I cannot say the agreement will be signed today or tomorrow," Moussa said. "(But) it is certain that there is great progress...towards a balanced agreement."
Moussa reiterated Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak's statement about the impact the Hebron agreement could have on the Israeli-Syrian track of the bilateral peace talks.
"President Mubarak clarified that the signing and fulfilling of an agreement (on Hebron) would positively affect the atmosphere of the peace process."
Other issues to be handled by the ministers include a border dispute between Qatar and Bahrain and the alliance's ties with its main two eastern neighbours -- Iraq and Iran.
Bahrain and Qatar have been at odds for decades over a cluster of small islands and sandbanks in the Gulf, controlled by Bahrain since the 1930s but also claimed by Qatar.
A GCC summit in the Qatari capital Doha this month, boycotted by Bahrian, decided to set up a committee to resolve the rift between the two Gulf states.
"The four-member committee formed to mediate between Qatar and Bahrain, will meet on Saturday...to set a framework for its work," said Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Saud al-Faisal.
Qatar has taken the case to the International Court of Justice in The Hague. The move has angered Bahrain, which prefers a regional solution.

Bahraini Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammad bin Mubarak al-Khalifa, commenting on the four-member committee, said: "Any meeting by brothers will be fruitful... and we are in favour of conciliation and agreement."
